source.title: A Rigorous, Tractable Measure of Model Complexity

record.tranche_reason: The paper revisits double-descent experiments and reports that the pattern persists for some model classes but is absent or attributable to changes in model complexity for others.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper's own Figure 4 experiments and reported comparisons of test error against GAC complexity. Statements about double descent cited from other studies are not recorded as results. Other experiments on complexity measures are outside the claim.
record.test_reason: The study reruns Belkin et al.'s MNIST double-descent sweeps (RFF, random forest, one-hidden-layer NN) and a CIFAR NN sweep, and adds gradient boosting. It then re-plots test error against its own complexity measure, GAC. The re-plot directly tests V7, the claim that double descent is an artifact of how complexity is counted. Double descent persists under GAC for constant-feature models but disappears for NN and boosting. The paper also argues that the GENP-V measure (Curth et al.) removes double descent by construction.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is largely correct. The authors conclude that double descent genuinely occurs for constant-feature models (RFF, random forests). For models whose features change during training (NN, gradient boosting), it is much less obvious, because GAC eventually decreases with capacity. The MNIST NN second descent may be an artifact of Belkin's initialization change. They also argue that GENP-V-based artifact claims are circular by construction.
record.recipe_differences: Revisits the MNIST experiments of Belkin et al. (2019), adding GAC comparisons; also revisits the CIFAR neural-network experiment with the same random initialization scheme for all sizes and adds CIFAR gradient boosting.
record.method_sensitivity: For the MNIST neural network, initialization differs between under- and over-parameterized regimes and the authors say this strongly affects GAC. For CIFAR, using one random initialization scheme across sizes still yields size-wise double descent, while plotting against GAC removes the pattern. Random-forest bootstrap resampling is disabled in the main experiment; the paper reports bootstrap-enabled results are conceptually unchanged.
record.problems: Figure 4 outcomes are mostly qualitative in the text, with plotted values rather than tabulated numeric results. The MNIST neural-network comparison changes initialization at the under-/over-parameterized transition, confounding that size sweep. The reported experiments do not test epochs or sample-size effects.
record.rows_left_out: No additional Figure 4 or Figure 7 result rows left out. Results from cited work and other figures that do not test the claim versions were omitted.

untested.parts: Deep (multi-layer) architectures. Only single-hidden-layer networks on 8×8 inputs were tested.
The study does not test whether a single effective-complexity measure predicts the peak location on any axis. GAC is used only to re-plot curves.
Label noise, regularization tuning, and multiple peaks are not studied.
Whether test error against GAC forms an ordinary U-shape is not stated. Only the disappearance of double descent is reported. The paper does not test ENP itself on these sweeps.

missing.what: Bootstrap-enabled random-forest results (test MSE vs leaves/trees and vs GAC), reported as conceptually unchanged
The argument that GENP-V and GENP-RX are defined through generalization error, so they show no double descent by construction. This is a T5 critique of the Curth et al. artifact claim.
missing.locator: Section 6, first paragraph; Section 4.1; Appendix C

missing.what: Training MSE curves showing where interpolation occurs in each sweep

record.verdict_notes: The GAC re-plots test the complexity-recounting question, which is V7, not V5 (peak-location prediction), so all GAC rows are relinked to V7. The result is split: V7 is challenged for constant-feature models and supported for changing-feature models. The paper is not an original source, though it replicates Belkin et al. (a V4 original). All outcomes are figure-only and qualitative. The networks are single-hidden-layer on 8×8 inputs, with 1000 training samples and 10 seeds.

versions.untested_parts: Epoch-wise behavior and effects of sample size are not tested.
No test-error sweep over training epochs.
No training-sample-size sweep near an interpolation threshold.
Interpolation thresholds are not explicitly located for every model class.
The reported complexity comparison concerns model-capacity sweeps; epochs and sample-size axes are not tested.
No systematic test of label noise, regularization tuning, or multiple/triple peaks.
The study does not measure against an effective number of parameters to test whether the second descent becomes an ordinary U-shape.

relation.reason: Its own capacity sweeps and error-versus-GAC comparisons directly bear on the claim versions.

tranche.reason: The study directly revisits double descent and argues that its interpretation depends on feature learning, initialization and the complexity measure.

source_check.notes: Both neural-network experiments use one hidden layer. For changing-feature models, total GAC is a loss-decrease-weighted aggregate across training (§5), rather than a literal effective parameter count.

statements.correction: Shallow MNIST network: second descent coincides with the warm-start/random-initialization transition; authors identify a possible artifact. This study does not move or remove the switch.
statements.problem: The initialization-switch coincidence is accurate, but this study supplies a scope limitation rather than an absence or reversal warranting challenges.

statements.correction: MNIST initialization changes at 10000 parameters, the stated interpolation transition for 10 classes and 1000 training examples; second descent occurs at that transition.
statements.problem: This study cannot distinguish following the initialization switch from following the interpolation point because the two coincide.

statements.correction: MNIST second descent coincides with the initialization change and may be an artifact; the appropriate study-specific interpretation is limits_scope.
statements.problem: The study accurately flags an initialization confound, but its observed second descent does not establish the effect absent or reversed.

statements.correction: MNIST forest: 10000 training and 10000 test examples; maximum leaves increase from 1 to 2000 with one tree, followed by increasing trees from 1 to 20 at 2000 leaves. The reported second descent concerns that combined axis.
statements.problem: The sample counts and single-tree segment are correct, but the prose reports second descent for a combined leaves-then-trees sweep rather than an isolated maximum-leaf sweep.

statements.correction: Forest second descent is reported for the combined maximum-leaves-then-tree-count axis with 10000 training and 10000 test examples. A separate leaf-only second descent is not established by the prose; the claimed conflict should be qualified accordingly.
statements.problem: The single-tree leaf-count second-descent claim overstates what the study's prose establishes.
